questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That they spoke english. And then what i thought of the courses, and how the university sounded when i researched them.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was way more stressfull then anticipated, and one of the courses was too time consuming compared to what I got out of it. But it wasn't all bad, so overall a 6/10

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Easy enough. They send us a lot of information, not all of it relevant to me, so I had a bit to sort through, but much of the information was there. The rest I could email them about

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was assigned a student advisor who I had to have a meeting with early on. Which was great, as I could email him about anything I was unsure of.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Easy enough. I got something within a week or two. But I maybe did say yes too quickly, as I hadn't looked at the transport time to my Campus. So I would recommend thinking more about location than I did, as I didn't think it mattered as much as it ended up doing.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It works pretty well

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were some discrepancy between which course catalog I was told i could choose from, and what courses was available to visiting students when the choosing process started. But I had been warned they could differ, so it was no big loss, just bummed one course wasn't available to me but it was to others.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I remember, when applying to the university, instead of a letter of recommendation (or something else that wasn't needed for me to send in) i had to attach a word document with courses i wished to have ranked from 1-10, with the top 1 pick with a high likelyhood of being approved. And it was. I think it was my 1st, 3rd and 4th pick I ended up getting. I could at most add 10 courses, but I only added 6ish. Then on the portal/website, it would show up which courses I got, wether each of the courses I had wished for had been approved. And when they did I was set. I emailed them early august, as I hadn't gotten courses, and they answered quickly with a course. And then I was all set

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: An email address. their website, and their course catalog.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Pretty successfull. Only one I didn't get.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Contact the host institution if you feel they need to do something soon to move the process along, but of course dont be annoying about it. Like email them if your missing just one course. I probably waited longer than necessary to email, as they updated my courses right away.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: third year courses

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
I think I work better with the structure we have in UCPH. But thats because I work best when there is more external structure, which I feel there is more of at UCPH than UoE. In addition, UoE had fewer of what they call tutorials, which are equivalent to our "class session" i.e. classes with 20-30 people. Most weeks were only lectures and Lab. 
They had no set coursebook only recommended reading, a few mandatory articles for assesments, and the lab manuals to read. So unlike UCPH I did not have to buy a specific book. I just showed up to lectures, and if I needed to know more, I could look at there recommended reading, which was often research articles, which were free to read, or google and find the info there.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Molecular genetics 3, molecular microbiology 3, Structures and functions of proteins 3

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Molecular microbiology 3. I did not know much about microbiology before, but I thought it was a good course. the hard part was that I had to write an essay that was 30% of my grade. We got a list of possible topics, and the one I picked, I knew nothing about but now I'm really glad I picked it as I learned a lot of interesting things. Molecular genetics 3 as well, but thats because the structure of that course was more similar to the structure back home. And the lab session we did was amazing, at least to me.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
I had to visit the dentist. Which I included in "personal spending". 
Memberships for society. All societies I looked at ranged from 5 pounds to 40. The sports ones tended to be more expensive
I spend way more on food than I had planned. But I did go out to eat or order takeout way more than I normally would, so that's why. I ended up spending twice as much on food than my planned budget, but that was a choice I made.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
groceries. I expected it to be cheaper, as I always hear about Denmark being more expensive to live in compared to other countries, but I feel like my money spend on groceries and food (eating out at a resturant or similar not included) was comparable to back home. 

I had set money aside in my budget for school books, but there was none for me, All we read were research articles, and those are free through the insititute, if not just online.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: UoE has some awesome societies! highly recommend joining a few.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: 100+ different societies, sports included. Theres everything from baking to badminton. Some based on activities, like hill walking, and others based on culture, like scandisociety, and then even more just aimed at international students

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join a society. Good way to try something new, and meet people

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Remember to relax and recharge. There is so much to do, its easy to do too much.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: A bit hard. But there was a lot of similarities

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Not really. UoE has so many international students, I mostly ended up hanging out with other international students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: They drive on the wrong side of the road. Nothing in particular stands out, but the whole "being in a different country alone, without people I know" was challenging.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The Ceilidh, which is the scottish folkdance. The friendliness

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Be aware what you need personally to make it a good stay. While you are there, how does your everyday look? does it work or does it need to change? are you focusing too much or too little on something? In that regards dont overstuff your calender, as it takes a lot of energy being in a different country, so you might not have the energy for all the new things and the old things.
2) the budget never works. Everyone i talked with ended up spending more than they had planned, so have some back up. But you could be better at budgeting then me, I might have been optimistic.
3) The things I enjoyed the most were the parts I was not expecting, so try something new you have no idea about, it might surprise you.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Remember to take breaks.
If you can, get there before the introweek. I got there 4 days before introweek, and that was not enough time to be settled, I feel, as the intro week is packed. But only as packed as you want, as nothing is mandatory (beside that one session on campus, thats either mandatory or just highly recommended to attend, as it has vital information)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Molecular microbiology 3, I learned most in that course, and might influence the master program I wanna do. 
The societies, I tried out different things, as many of them have free events in the first week.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Managing my time. I should have spend more time looking at my energy levels, and not just the things I wanted to do.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
